title: Allahabad HC: A 159-Page Order That Only Copies the Award Is Not a Reasoned Order
seo_title: Allahabad HC Sets Aside Order Copying Arbitral Award
meta_description: Allahabad HC sets aside a Commercial Court order against Penguin Random House: a long Section 34 order copying the award is not a reasoned one.
bench: Chief Justice Arun Bhansali and Justice Kshitij Shailendra
case_name: Penguin Random House India Private Limited v. Mindmill Software Limited
citation: Appeal Under Section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 No. 34 of 2024, reserved on 27.10.2026, delivered on 04.11.2026
body: A commercial court in Gautam Budh Nagar wrote an order running to 159 pages to dismiss an arbitration challenge, and the Allahabad High Court has now told it to do the job again, properly this time. The ruling is a reminder that a long order and a reasoned order are not the same thing, and that courts deciding arbitration challenges cannot get away with simply copying out the award and the parties' written arguments.

The dispute traces back to a commercial lease. Mindmill Software Limited let out premises to Penguin Random House India Private Limited under an unregistered lease dated 28 March 2008, for a three year term starting 1 April 2008. When the lease period ended on 23 May 2010, Penguin Random House did not hand back possession. Mindmill kept raising monthly bills of five lakh rupees for the premises, and Penguin Random House paid those bills only up to March 2011. The disagreement over what followed went to arbitration, and an award was eventually passed against Penguin Random House.

Penguin Random House challenged that award under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, in Arbitration Objection Case No. 7 of 2012 before the Commercial Court, Gautam Budh Nagar. On 8 December 2023, the Commercial Court dismissed those objections. The order it passed ran to 159 pages, and that length became the problem rather than a mark of thoroughness.

On appeal under Section 37, the Allahabad High Court bench of Chief Justice Arun Bhansali and Justice Kshitij Shailendra went through what those 159 pages actually contained. Pages 6 to 84, the court found, did nothing more than reproduce paragraphs 123 to 345 of the arbitral award itself. Pages 86 to 142 reproduced the written submissions filed by the parties, in full. What was left, once the copied material was set aside, did not amount to an examination of whether the award deserved to be set aside or upheld.

The bench's conclusion was direct: the merits of the challenge to the award had not been examined at all, and an order of that kind cannot stand merely because it runs to many pages. Reasoning is not measured by volume. A commercial court hearing a Section 34 objection has one central job, which is to test the award against the narrow grounds the statute allows, and reproducing the award or the submissions is not a substitute for that exercise, however long the resulting document turns out to be.

Having found the order unsustainable on that basis, the High Court allowed Penguin Random House's appeal, set aside the Commercial Court's order of 8 December 2023, and sent the Section 34 objections back to the Commercial Court, Gautam Budh Nagar, to be decided afresh. The bench was careful not to say anything about whether the award itself was right or wrong, since doing so at this stage could have unfairly tilted the fresh hearing in favour of one side or the other. That restraint means neither party has won anything substantive yet. Penguin Random House has only won a proper hearing of its objections, which is not a small thing after waiting since 2012 for one, but it is also not the end of the matter.

For litigants before the commercial courts set up under the Commercial Courts Act, this ruling is a useful marker of what a Section 34 order needs to show on its face. Parties who have invested years and money in an arbitration, and then in a Section 34 challenge, are entitled to know that a judge actually weighed their specific grounds, whether those grounds concern the arbitrator's jurisdiction, patent illegality, or a conflict with the fundamental policy of Indian law. An order that recites the award and the submissions without engaging with either leaves that question unanswered, and an appellate court can send the case straight back rather than wade into the merits itself.

The case also illustrates a cost that foreign-owned companies operating through Indian subsidiaries run into often enough in commercial litigation here: a straightforward landlord-tenant billing dispute from 2010 and 2011 produced an arbitration, then a Section 34 challenge filed in 2012, then thirteen years before the Commercial Court ruled on it, and now a remand that starts the clock again on the Section 37 stage. Penguin Random House India, part of a global publishing group, will go back to square one before the same Commercial Court, this time expecting a decision that actually grapples with its arguments rather than restating them.
why_it_matters: A Section 34 challenge to an arbitral award is often the only chance a party gets to have a court test the award before it becomes enforceable, and this ruling confirms that an order rejecting such a challenge must show real engagement with the grounds raised, not just reproduce the award and the submissions at length. For any company, including a foreign-owned Indian subsidiary, contesting an award before a commercial court, it is a reminder that a dismissal of a Section 34 petition can itself be challenged on the quality of its reasoning, independent of whether the award was right.
card_summary: Allahabad HC sets aside a 159-page Commercial Court order against Penguin Random House, finding it only copied the arbitral award and the parties' submissions without examining the Section 34 challenge on its merits.
card_tip: A long order rejecting your Section 34 objections is not automatically a reasoned one; if it mainly reproduces the award and the submissions, that is itself a ground for appeal under Section 37.
